newsitem.title: USA: Mutual Funds -- how many is too many? too few?.
newsitem.headline: Mutual Funds -- how many is too many? too few?.

text.p: How many stock-buying mutual funds should you hold? And how should they work together?

Now that many investors are already in the mutual fund market, and are perhaps being seduced by the number of new and newly-hyped offerings every month, this question has taken on increased importance.

In the old days, financial experts used to answer this question by figuring out how much money you had. With $10,000 or less, you should own one or two funds, said the pros. Between $10,000 and $50,000, you might want five funds. More than that, and ten funds would be a reasonable amount of funds to own.

But now, experts are researching this question in a more analytical way. They are studying the marketplace to try to determine an optimum number of funds that could deliver higher returns at lower risks and lower costs.

One such academician is Edward O'Neal, an assistant professor of finance at the University of New Hampshire. O'Neal studied the question of whether it makes sense to own several different funds in the same investment category. In other words, if you are buying a growth fund, are you better off buying five growth funds? Or 20? There are more than 1,000 funds out there that call themselves growth funds.

O'Neal created a variety of sample portfolios of funds holding as few as one fund and as many as 30. He found that there was significant benefit in holding five funds instead of just one, and a somewhat smaller additional benefit to holding 10 funds instead of five.

The benefits, according to O'Neal, were that if you held a greater number of funds, you had a greater chance of meeting your investment goals. In technical terms, the dispersion of terminal wealth -- the money that accumulated over the holding period -- was greatly reduced as more funds were added, say up to 10 funds. The benefits of adding another five, 10 or 20 funds were negligible.

Morningstar, a Chicago fund research firm, takes a similar perspective on the how-many-funds question. Analyst Catherine Voss Sanders reports that adding funds to a portfolio tends to narrow the range of results and decrease the volatility. It also, according to Sanders, "reduces your shot at the top." If you are a high flyer who doesn't mind risk but wants to try for tippy-top results, adding funds will hurt your chances. That's not a strategy many would advocate, though.

Sanders, like O'Neal, finds that the biggest benefits of diversification come from holding about four or five stock funds, and that there is some added benefit to holding another four or five. Then it levels off.

If you decide to hold four or five different stock funds, how do you select them for maximum benefit? First, look for funds that have low costs in terms of management fees and no buried marketing charges, called 12(b)1 fees -- if you fragment your money among several different funds, and pay high fees for each one, that can skim most of your benefit off the top.

Second, you might try to buy funds that aim for different sectors of the market -- a small stock fund and a large stock fund, for example. Or one fund that goes for fast growing stocks and another that looks for bargains.

Third, here's a word of caution: If you decide to diversify among several funds, read their annual reports of holdings to make sure you are really diversified. Buying five funds doesn't do much for you if all five funds are most heavily invested in the same stocks.

Finally, Sanders reminds that if you are willing to buy one fund that is broad enough, you can ignore much of the fund diversification advice. An index fund that buys the broader stock market and not just the Standard & Poor's 500, for example, can go a long way toward reducing risk and hitting growth targets at a minimum of expenses.
Sanders gets the last word with her bit of closing advice: Buy the number of funds that make you happy.
"Not everyone is a fund junkie" she concedes. If you don't want to deal with it all, look for one low-cost, well-managed fund and stop spending your time reading academic studies.
